excerpt_original: His portraits of Black communities in the American South, made throughout the 1980s, established Baldwin Lee as one of the defining figures of American documentary photography. It is an overlooked New York body of work, photographed in the 1970s, that the Howard Greenberg…

blocks.text: Before the South, there was New York. And before the portraits, the vast emptiness of its architectural structures. Born in 1951, Baldwin Lee grew up in Manhattan’s Chinatown. He first studied under Minor White, a presiding figure of contemplative photography, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, before going on to Yale, where Walker Evans’s teaching — Evans being the undisputed reference of American documentary photography — completed the formation of his eye. “I would tell my students that my photography teachers, White and Evans, were the equivalent of having studied with Matisse and Cézanne,” he recalls in an interview with Jessica Bell Brown published in Baldwin Lee (Hunters Point Press, 2022).

After graduating in 1975, he returned again and again to the city of his childhood, a 4×5 view camera on a tripod over his shoulder, moving through Manhattan at dawn, often in winter, when the sidewalks emptied of their inhabitants. “My trips to New York City from New England were an exploration of buildings as organic forms,” the artist confides. “Rather than approaching the work as architectural photography, I saw it as a way of capturing a landscape. It was my first time using a large-format camera. Early in the morning, with no one around, I felt an overwhelming intimacy — as if I were walking through my own private garden.”

His subjects include Wall Street at dawn, Times Square, and the streets and vacant lots of Lower Manhattan where the World Trade Center looms in the distance. Baldwin Lee records a city suspended between neglect and ambition, where remnants of the past remain visible alongside the structures of the new. Worn brick facades, Cadillac Eldorados parked along the curb, the twin towers still new: these images carry the trace of a human presence temporarily absent but not gone. “If the buildings were people it would be acceptable if they did not speak,” he tells Blind. “The silence can be a metaphor for spaces, once occupied, now vacant. The lack of people points to an unfulfilled potential.”

blocks.text: Baldwin Lee went on to teach at Yale, then at the Massachusetts College of Art. In 1982, he moved to Knoxville, Tennessee, where he founded the photography program at the university, which he would lead for more than thirty years. The following year, he embarked on an extensive series of journeys through the American South. Between 1983 and 1989, he made nearly ten thousand photographs, principally of Black communities — a body of work celebrated as a major social testament to rural Black America. “The photographs I made in the South would never have come about without adequate education and awareness: North/South, Black/white, male/female, private/public, poor/rich, powerful/subjugated,” he tells Jessica Bell Brown.

The New York photographs reveal a different but related aspect of Baldwin Lee’s practice. Their careful organization of architectural space and sustained attention to the character of place helped establish the distinctive visual language he would carry into his later work. They demonstrate a sensitivity to form and order, but also to the humanity inscribed in the built environment. His vision of New York is a record of what people made, inhabited, altered, and left behind.

blocks.text: The prints selected for the exhibition present his images at a scale he has never seen before. “No, I have not seen them printed at that scale,” he confides to Blind. “At this large scale the photographs and the viewer have a different relationship. A dialog between the photograph is possible and encouraged. The viewer is now capable of entering the space of the photo making for a more intimate experience.”
The twin towers that dominate several of his images have since vanished from the New York sky. The city Baldwin Lee once photographed as his own private garden no longer exists.

blocks.text: “Baldwin Lee: New York (1975–1979)” is on show at the Howard Greenberg Gallery from September 18, 2026 to October 31, 2026.
A reception with the artist will be held at the Howard Greenberg Gallery on Thursday, September 17, 2026 from 5:00 to 7:00 p.m.
Baldwin Lee is published by Hunters Point Press (2022).
